thesis: The episode argues that Wish's business model is unsustainable because it requires excessive marketing spend to retain users who leave after a single purchase, resulting in negative operating cash flow. In contrast, the discussion highlights Pinduodua's success in achieving marketing leverage by significantly reducing its marketing spend as a percentage of revenue. The broader theme suggests that current e-commerce players often fail to habituate consumers or solve fundamental value proposition issues, relying instead on promotions that do not drive sustainable growth.

claims.claim: The business model is unsustainable because high maintenance marketing spend is required to retain users who leave after one purchase.
claims.quote: Whereas wish buyers buy once and are just done with them. Whatever they, that's, experience was that was not right for them and they're gone. But if you give them 50 off, then sure, sure, they'll find some crap that they could buy again.

claims.claim: Spending over 30% of revenue on marketing just to keep existing customers makes profitability highly unlikely.
claims.quote: But it just seems very far-fetched when you're spending 30 plus percent of revenues just to keep your existing customers. That is such a high bar to overcome and to still be profitable. It just seems very unlikely.

claims.quote: And Etsy is that is a big problem they're having, which is trying to constantly reengage users that maybe they bought something last year, but they didn't buy something this year, and trying to get that hurdle.

claims.quote: Obviously, Amazon goes through tremendous lengths to have such a valuable Amazon Prime bundle that they're always top of mind and you're exceedingly habituated check Amazon first.

claims.quote: For example, Lyfts sometimes does when they're saying 20% off the next three rides or Postmates or DoorDash does when they say, here's a $10 credit when you order with us.

claims.claim: The business model is flawed because high marketing spend fails to drive growth, indicating a disconnect between the product value proposition and consumer needs.
claims.quote: If you were spending some 80% of your revenues for 2% revenue growth and are unprofitable, that is never going to be a recipe for success. We could even skip the cohort analysis that we're going to do later. That alone would tell you there's something deeply wrong with this business.

claims.claim: Wish failed to habituate consumers, unlike successful platforms, and tried to solve fundamental value prop issues with promotions instead of better selection or quality.
claims.quote: These are not customers that are habituated to use wish. They are not saying that I love the value prop of Wish so much that what they offer on its own is in it of itself sufficient to compel me to be an ongoing customer. What they're basically saying is that I'm not going to shop on the site unless you continue to give me 50 off promos.
